You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 66
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Curriculum Designer
- Trauma Type: Combat
- Pcl5: 49

# Margaret's Careful Mornings

Margaret sits at her kitchen table with her coffee growing cold, watching the garden through the window. At sixty-six, she has learned that mornings require a particular kind of vigilance. She needs to be awake for at least twenty minutes before she tries to do anything that matters—before she opens her laptop to work on the curriculum materials due to her team by noon, before she calls her daughter, before she allows herself to believe the day might unfold normally.

Fifty-three years have passed since she served as a combat medic in the Pacific theater, but her body hasn't seemed to notice the decades. The dreams still come most nights—the smell of blood and diesel fuel, the weight of a soldier's leg in her hands as she applied a tourniquet, the sound of helicopters that never quite landed. She wakes sometimes gasping, her heart moving so fast she has to sit on the edge of the bed and count her breaths until her hands stop shaking.

Her work as a curriculum designer suits her in ways she didn't expect when she took the position eight years ago. There's something calming about structuring learning, about building frameworks that help people understand complex ideas. She designs online courses for healthcare workers, and there's an irony she doesn't discuss with her colleagues—she's designing training modules for people who will face emergencies she knows intimately. Last month, she spent three weeks developing a module on trauma response for nurses. She rewrote the section on emotional regulation five times, each version drawing from knowledge she's accumulated through her own relentless effort to stay functional.

But structure only holds so much. Last Tuesday, a notification sound on her computer—a sharp electronic beep she'd never heard before—sent her into a state of such acute panic that she had to excuse herself from a video meeting. She sat in her bedroom for forty minutes, unable to explain to her team why she'd disappeared. The sound had triggered something primal, something that insisted danger was immediate and real. She knows intellectually that a notification isn't a warning siren, but her nervous system disagrees with a certainty that no amount of reasoning can touch.

Her ex-husband used to say she was "difficult to live with," which was his way of describing the nights she'd wake him with her thrashing, or the afternoons when she'd snap at him over something trivial because she was already running at half-capacity just managing the background noise of her own anxiety. The divorce was finalized fourteen years ago. She doesn't blame him anymore, though she used to.

Margaret has learned to build her life around the unpredictability of her own mind. She takes the same route to the grocery store because unfamiliar environments require too much cognitive energy. She keeps her schedule light and avoids crowds. She has three friends she trusts, and she sees them individually, never in groups. She's learned which restaurants have exits she can see from her table. She's learned to recognize the feeling of dissociation before it fully arrives—a kind of cottony distance from her own hands—and she has techniques to ground herself: touching something cold, naming five things she can see.

The coffee is definitely cold now. Margaret pours it down the sink and makes a fresh cup. Her team is expecting the curriculum module by noon, and she's nearly finished. She opens her laptop, takes a breath, and begins to type. The work steadies her. It always does. She has learned, over these long decades, that productivity and presence are not the same thing as healing, but they are something. They are enough to keep her moving forward, even on mornings when forward feels like the hardest direction to go.
